subsection: 2. Modes of communication and the impact of technology

notes.b: A mode (also called a medium) is the method used to deliver a message from the sender to the receiver, who may then send feedback (a response). Choosing the right mode matters because the same message can succeed or fail depending on how it is delivered.
points: Verbal communication uses spoken words, including phone and video calls. Non-verbal communication uses the body, face, tone of voice and eye contact. Written communication keeps words as a record, and visual communication uses images, charts and diagrams.

A mode can be one-way (such as a notice, where the receiver cannot reply on the spot) or two-way (such as a discussion, where feedback flows straight back), and it can be formal or informal depending on the setting.

Each mode can be judged by how it copes with barriers, the things that stop a message being understood, such as information overload (too many messages to take in), the wrong medium for the message, and differences of culture or language.

Efficacy means how well a mode achieves its communication goal. It is different from efficiency, which is about speed and cost, so a cheap, fast mode can still be inefficacious if the message is not understood.
notes.tip: Keep efficacy (does the mode meet its goal?) separate from efficiency (speed and cost). A video call is verbal with non-verbal cues visible, and a report can be both written and visual.

notes.b: Verbal communication uses spoken words and is the most immediate form of workplace communication. Its main weakness is that speech disappears once it is said.
points: Face-to-face communication allows immediate feedback and the full range of cues (tone, expression, gesture), so it suits sensitive or complex discussions.
Meetings bring several people together to share information or make decisions, but they take time and can be dominated by a few voices, so quieter members may not contribute.
Telephone calls allow quick two-way discussion when people are apart, but they give no visual cues and leave no record unless notes are kept.
Video calls combine speech with visible facial expressions and gestures, which helps when teams are spread across locations.
Verbal communication leaves no permanent record, so decisions reached in conversation often need written confirmation to avoid later disagreement about what was agreed.
notes.tip: A common mistake is to treat a video call as non-verbal. It uses spoken words, so it is verbal, with non-verbal cues visible.

notes.b: Non-verbal communication conveys meaning through the body, face and tone of voice, and it can be as strong as the words used.
points: Body language, such as posture and gestures, signals confidence, interest or unease. A speaker who slouches and avoids the audience may seem unsure whatever they say.
Facial expressions show emotional response, and a listener may read a frown as disagreement even when the words are neutral.
Tone of voice, pace and volume communicate attitude and urgency, so the same words can sound supportive or hostile.
Eye contact shows attention and sincerity to many listeners, although its meaning varies across cultures, so it should not be read the same way for everyone.
Non-verbal cues are hard to control and can contradict the spoken message, which undermines trust when the two do not match.
notes.tip: Do not quote a percentage split between words, tone and body language. It is unverified and a known misreading of research.

notes.b: Written communication creates a lasting record and can reach many people, but it gives limited opportunity for an immediate response.
points: Email is fast, cheap and easy to send to many recipients, and it creates a searchable record that can be checked later.
Email is often overused, which leads to information overload (more messages than people can handle) and slow responses to matters that need urgent attention.
Instant messaging suits quick, informal exchanges between team members, but messages can be ignored or misread without tone of voice.
Reports present detailed information in a structured form that can be referred back to, but they take time to prepare and to read.
Noticeboards, intranet posts (the organisation's private website) and newsletters reach a wide audience at low cost, but they offer no direct response.
notes.tip: Describe the type of tool (a messaging tool, a video-call tool) rather than naming a product. A written mode is words kept as a record, which is different from a visual mode.

notes.b: Visual communication uses images, charts and diagrams to show information quickly and clearly.
points: Charts and graphs make trends and comparisons easy to grasp, so they suit reporting numerical performance.
Diagrams and flowcharts show processes or structures, which helps staff follow a new procedure step by step.
Presentations combine slides, images and speech and can hold an audience's attention, but slides overloaded with text reduce clarity.
Videos and infographics (images and short text combined to explain a topic) engage people who learn best visually and can be shared widely, though producing good-quality content takes time and money.

notes.b: The right mode depends on the message, the audience and the situation, so a manager should weigh several criteria together rather than pick a favourite mode.
points: Urgency: urgent messages need a fast mode, such as a phone call or face-to-face meeting, because a slow mode could let the problem grow.
Cost: a mode should be chosen with its cost in mind, since a meeting for a large group costs more than an email.
Confidentiality: sensitive information should go through a private, secure mode, such as a one-to-one meeting or encrypted email (email scrambled so only the intended reader can open it).
Audience: the number, location and preferences of recipients determine whether a mode will reach them effectively.
Need for a record: messages that must be referred to later, such as agreed targets, suit a written mode.
Complexity: complicated information is easier to understand in a mode that allows questions, such as a meeting, than in a short message.
Feedback: where a response is needed, a two-way mode such as a discussion is better than a one-way notice.
The criteria often pull in different directions, so the best answer is often a combination, such as a live two-way session backed by a written summary that gives a record.
notes.tip: If asked to outline considerations when choosing a mode, name the criteria (for example urgency and confidentiality), not modes, and say in a line why each matters for the message given. Develop only as many as the question asks. Scenarios usually suit a combined approach justified by the criteria.

notes.b: Efficacy means how well a mode achieves its communication goal. Each mode has strengths and weaknesses, so analysing efficacy means weighing both for a given message and audience.
points: Face-to-face communication is highly effective for building trust and handling complex issues, but it is slow and costly when people are far apart.
Email is effective for detailed, recorded messages to many people, but it can be ignored or buried in an overloaded inbox.
Video calls are effective for remote teams and two-way discussion, but poor connections and screen fatigue (tiredness from long spells on screen) reduce their effect.
Noticeboards are cheap and reach everyone in a location, but they are weak for complex or sensitive messages and cannot confirm receipt, because there is no way to know who has read them.
Visual presentations are effective for explaining data, but they fail if the audience cannot see or interpret the visuals.
notes.tip: For identify and analyse questions, name the mode first, then give its strengths and weaknesses for the message and audience in the question, for example confidential news to a dispersed workforce.

notes.b: Technology has changed communication across eight parameters: modes, speed, cost, access, collaboration, sustainable practices, productivity and security. Each has a positive and a negative side. The specification describes disruptive impact as how digital technology can change the way businesses operate and how consumers interact with them, for better or worse.
points: Modes: technology has added video calls, instant messaging and collaboration platforms (online spaces where teams work together), giving more options but more choices to manage.
Speed: messages and files can be sent instantly, which speeds up decisions, but expectations of immediate replies can add pressure.
Cost: digital communication is usually cheaper than printing and travel, though subscriptions, devices and support carry their own costs.
Access: cloud tools (software and storage reached over the internet) let staff reach information from anywhere, but people without reliable internet or digital skills can be excluded.
Collaboration: shared documents and platforms let many people edit and comment on the same work in real time.
Sustainable practices: digital communication reduces paper and travel, but data centres and devices use energy and create electronic waste.
Productivity: tools that automate routine messages and scheduling save time, but constant notifications interrupt focused work.
Security: digital systems face phishing, malware and data breaches, so organisations need strong passwords, staff training and access controls.
notes.tip: Do not quote figures for email volumes, costs, time lost to notifications or energy use. Name parameters with their effect on the business, give a positive and a negative for each, and avoid listing only positives.

notes.b: Security is part of communication, not a separate IT matter, because a message that is intercepted, faked or lost has failed in its purpose. Three terms are easily confused.
points: Phishing is a fraudulent message that tries to trick the recipient into revealing data or clicking a harmful link. Staff training helps because the attack targets people, not just machines.
Malware is harmful software that damages systems or steals data. Strong passwords and access controls limit what it can reach.
A data breach is unauthorised access to, or loss of, data. Access controls (rules on who may see what) reduce the damage if one account is compromised.

Irish Examiner, 15 September 2026, reporting the Hiscox Cyber Readiness Report 2026: in a survey of 300 Irish firms with fewer than 250 staff, those hit by a successful attack averaged 34 hours of operational disruption in 12 months, and 36% lost business opportunities or partnerships.
notes.tip: Use the 2026 Hiscox example for security, phishing, staff training and access controls, quoted with its source and date. Do not use the HSE cyber attack of May 2021 or any other named attack, and do not quote a cyber-insurance percentage.

notes.h: Technology, the wider organisation and ethics
notes.b: Digital tools change how organisations design their communication, and they raise ethical and business considerations about privacy, fairness and the environment.
points: Digital transformation means redesigning communication processes around digital tools, so knowledge can be shared across departments and locations.

Personal data is information about an identifiable person. Data protection rules, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, an EU regulation applying since 25 May 2018), apply to workplace messages that contain personal data, so organisations must control who can see what. This is an ethical duty to protect privacy.
A communication policy sets out which tools to use for which purposes, which reduces confusion and protects data.
Digital communication can also help small firms reach customers and partners cheaply, for example through social media.
Ethical issues include privacy, honest use of monitoring of staff, and including staff who lack digital access, who may miss messages sent only online.
Sustainability cuts both ways: paperless communication and reduced travel save resources, but data centres and devices use energy and create electronic waste.

Irish Examiner, 14 August 2026: an IReach survey of 1,000 adults for NFP Ireland, an Aon company, found 30% of workers believe their role is safe from AI or automation over the next decade and 23% say large parts of their job are likely to disappear.
NFP's Colm Power said employers should communicate openly about how AI will affect roles and involve staff early, before rolling out new tools.
notes.tip: Use the 2026 AI example for managing change, ongoing engagement, two-way channels and ethics, and treat the figures as the survey's, quoted with source and date. A news task asks you to link an item to a point and give an opinion supported by a reason.

notes.b: A discuss or evaluate question wants a balanced review that ends in a judgement, not a list of parameters. Technology enables communication by making it faster and cheaper, but the benefit is not automatic.
points: Your judgement should weigh the gains against the costs: instant, low-cost, shared tools let people communicate across locations and work on the same material together, so decisions are quicker and more people can take part.

The benefit depends on managing overload, because more modes and constant messages can bury important ones and interrupt focus. It also depends on treating security as part of communication, so messages and personal data stay protected.
It depends too on inclusion: staff or customers without reliable internet or digital skills need another way to receive messages.

A good answer applies these points to the business named, for example a Dublin software company (a sample business) with staff in several locations: collaboration and speed gain, while phishing and notification overload need policies and training.
notes.tip: Cover several of the eight parameters, each with a positive and a negative, apply them to the business in the question, and finish with a judgement and what it depends on. Common mistakes are giving only positives, naming parameters with no effect, and treating security as a separate IT matter.

keyTerms.definition: Communication that uses spoken words, in person, by telephone or by video call.
Communication conveyed through body language, facial expression, tone of voice and eye contact rather than through words.
The posture, gestures and movements that signal a person's attitude or feelings.
Communication that uses written words, such as email, messages, reports and notices, and that can be kept as a record.
How well a mode of communication achieves its intended goal.
A fraudulent message that tries to trick the recipient into revealing data or clicking a harmful link.
Redesigning how an organisation works and communicates around digital technology.
A written set of rules on which tools to use for different purposes and how information is handled.

Face-to-face conversation, meetings, telephone calls and video calls.
Email, instant messages, reports, noticeboards and intranet posts; charts, diagrams, presentations and videos.

Body language, facial expression, tone of voice and eye contact.

questions.prompt: A Dublin software company must tell all staff about a change to their pension scheme. Identify the factors that should guide the choice of communication mode, and explain why they matter in this case.
questions.model: Confidentiality matters because pension details are personal, so the company should use a private channel, such as individual emails or a one-to-one meeting, rather than a public noticeboard. The number and location of staff also matter: a company-wide video briefing reaches everyone at once, including remote workers, and allows questions. Finally, the need for a record matters because the details of the scheme must be referred to later, so a written summary should follow the briefing. Together these factors point to a combined approach: a live two-way session for explanation and questions, backed up by a written document that staff can keep.

questions.prompt: Assess how digital technology has changed communication in an Irish retail business across speed, cost and security, and evaluate whether the overall effect has been positive.
questions.model: Speed has improved, because managers can send stock updates or pricing changes to every store in seconds, and staff can get answers without waiting for post or a meeting. This allows faster decisions, although constant messages can create pressure to reply instantly and can overwhelm staff who work on shop floors. Cost has fallen, since email and instant messaging replace printing, couriers and many travel costs, which matters for a chain with stores spread across the country. However, the business pays for subscriptions, devices and support, so the saving is real but not total. Security is the area of greatest risk. Digital communication exposes customer card details, staff records and supplier data to phishing and malware, and a single careless click can cause a serious breach. The business must therefore invest in passwords, staff training and access controls. On balance, the effect has been positive, because faster and cheaper communication improves operations and responsiveness. But the gains depend on managing message overload and on treating security as part of communication, not as a separate IT issue.
